The background is light purple with a network of glowing nodes and lines, suggesting a digital or security theme. What is Authorization? Authorization is the process of determining whether a user has the right to access a resource or perform an action, based on rules, roles, or policies. In IAM context: Happens after authentication (proving identity) Focuses on what you can do once you're in Examples: Can a user access a file, database, or service? Can an employee approve expenses or modify records? Driven by: Access control models: RBAC, ABAC, PBAC Business roles, policies, and compliance needs

Access Control Model Definition An Access Control Model is a structured framework that defines how permissions are assigned and enforced to control access to digital resources. Mechanism Rather than assigning permissions directly to individual users, an access control model uses rules, roles, attributes, or policies to determine: • Who can access • What resources • Under what conditions

PBAC architectures 1 PEP – Policy Enforcement Point Intercepts user requests and enforces access decisions 2 PDP – Policy Decision Point Evaluates access requests against policies and returns allow/deny 3 PAP – Policy Administration Point The interface or tool where policies are created, managed, and stored 4 PIP – Policy Information Point Provides external attributes or context needed for decisions graph TD
 User((user)) -- "request access" --> PEP[PEP Enforce Policies]
 PEP --> Resource[Resource]
 PEP -- "can this user Access Resource?" --> PDP[PDP Evaluate Policies]
 PDP -- "YES/NO" --> PEP
 SecurityAdmin((Security Admin)) -- "create policy" --> PAP[PAP Manage Policies]
 PAP --> PDP
 PDP --> PIP[PIP Retrieve additional Attributes]
 PIP --> PDP
 PIP --- Context[Context: Org Chart, Cloud, DB] The diagram illustrates the PBAC architecture components and their interactions. A user requests access to a resource, which is intercepted by the PEP (Policy Enforcement Point). The PEP then asks the PDP (Policy Decision Point) if the user can access the resource. The PDP evaluates the request and returns a YES/NO decision to the PEP. The PEP then enforces the decision and either grants access to the resource or denies it. The PDP is also responsible for managing policies, which are created by the PAP (Policy Administration Point). The PAP is managed by a Security Admin. The PDP also interacts with the PIP (Policy Information Point) to retrieve additional attributes needed for decisions. The PIP is connected to various data sources, including an organization chart, a cloud, and a database. Diagram of PBAC architecture showing the flow between PEP, PDP, PAP, and PIP. Critical for Zero Trust and modern IAM

Additional Access Control Models 1 DAC – Discretionary Access Control Permissions are set by the resource owner. → Users decide who can access their files or resources. 2 MAC – Mandatory Access Control Permissions are based on system-enforced rules and classifications. → Users can't change access rights (common in military or government systems). 3 ReBAC – Relationship-Based Access Control Access is determined by the relationship between entities. → Example: A doctor can access a patient's records if assigned to them. 4 Context-Aware Access Control Access decisions include contextual factors. → Time, location, device type, risk score, etc.

Summary ✓ Access control models define how permissions are granted: - RBAC: Role-based, scalable and simple - ABAC: Attribute-based, more flexible - PBAC: Policy-based, context-aware and dynamic ✓ Authorization is a legal requirement in Europe: - GDPR, CNIL, ISO 27001 emphasize access control, role definition, and auditability ✓ Privileged Access Management (PAM): - Focuses on high-risk accounts with elevated permissions - Implements JIT access, session monitoring, vaulting ✓ Policy-Based Access Architecture (PEP, PDP, PAP, PIP): - PEP: Enforces decisions - PDP: Makes decisions - PAP: Defines policies - PIP: Provides identity and context information ✓ Best Practice: Choose access control models that align with business needs, compliance, and risk posture The diagram illustrates the relationship between three access control models: RBAC, ABAC, and PBAC.
